p.src: The story goes that Abbot Zhizhen said that day, “Zhishen, you absolutely cannot remain here. I have a junior brother who is now abbot of the Great Xiangguo Temple in the Eastern Capital. He is called Chan Master Zhiqing. I shall give you a letter to take to him, so that you may seek a post as a working monk there. Last night I discerned your future and composed four lines of verse for you. They will serve you throughout your life, so remember what I tell you today.” Zhishen knelt and said, “I am ready to hear the verse.” The abbot said, “Meeting a forest, you shall rise; meeting a mountain, you shall prosper; meeting water, you shall flourish; meeting a river, you shall come to rest.” After hearing the four-line verse, Lu Zhishen bowed nine times to the abbot. He shouldered his bundle, waist pouch, and belly pouch, concealed the letter, and took leave of the abbot and all the monks. After descending Mount Wutai, he went straight to an inn beside the smithy and lodged there, waiting for his monk’s staff and戒刀 to be forged; once everything was ready, he would depart. When the monks in the temple learned that Lu Zhishen had gone, not one of them failed to rejoice. The abbot ordered the lay brothers who tended the fires to clear away the damaged Guardian Kings Pavilion themselves. Within a few days, Squire Zhao personally brought a quantity of money and goods to Mount Wutai. The Guardian Kings were sculpted anew and the pavilion halfway up the mountain rebuilt, but of that no more need be said. A poem bears witness:

p.src: Leaving one Zen grove, he enters another; meeting a kindred soul, their loyalty can sever gold. For now his awesome might shall chill the bandits’ hearts; why use subtle doctrine merely to delight a monkish mind? Long has his sobriquet been the Flowery Monk; by religious name he is called Lu Zhishen. When worldly vows are fulfilled, at last he shall attain the fruit; yet for the present, alas, he finds no understanding friend.

He rewarded the smith with some fragments of silver, shouldered his bundle, girded on the戒刀, and took up the monk’s staff. Then, bidding farewell to the innkeeper and the smith, he set out upon his journey. Those who passed him on the road saw that he was truly a fierce and reckless monk. Indeed, behold:

p.src: His black monk’s robe is worn with both arms through its sleeves; a round green cord is tied askew, its twin ends knotted. Within its sheath, his戒刀 conceals three feet of spring ice; Upon his shoulder, his monk’s staff lies like a great iron python. His heron-like legs are tightly bound in gaiters; his spider belly is firmly girded with robe and alms bowl. Around his lips bristle a thousand clipped iron wires; across his chest lies a band of hair stout enough to shield his gall. Born with the face of one who devours meat and fish, he is no reader of sutras or chanter of Buddha’s name.

p.src: The mountain shadows deepen, and the shade of the scholar trees slowly fades. Beyond the green willows, birds are heard returning to the woods; Within the village of red apricot blossoms, cattle and sheep are seen entering their pens. The setting sun, wreathed in smoke, raises an emerald mist; broken clouds reflect upon the water and scatter crimson light. Beside the stream, an old fisherman poles his boat away; across the fields, a village boy rides home astride a calf.

Within the village of red apricot blossoms, cattle and sheep are seen entering their pens.

Beside the stream, an old fisherman poles his boat away; across the fields, a village boy rides home astride a calf.

p.src: Because Lu Zhishen had been captivated by the lovely scenery, he had wandered on for half the day and failed to reach a lodging place. With no companion on the road, where could he spend the night? He pressed on another twenty or thirty li and crossed a plank bridge. Far away, beneath a bank of crimson clouds, he glimpsed a manor flashing into view amid a grove of trees; behind it rose layer upon layer of rugged hills. Lu Zhishen said, “I have no choice but to ask for lodging at that manor.” He hurried straight to the manor and saw several dozen farmhands bustling anxiously about, carrying things this way and that. At the gate, Lu Zhishen leaned his monk’s staff aside and saluted the servants of the manor. One of them said, “Monk, what are you doing at our manor so late in the day?” Zhishen replied, “I could not reach a lodging place. I wish to pass one night at your honored manor and shall leave early tomorrow.” The man said, “Something is happening at our manor tonight. You cannot stay here.” Zhishen said, “Just let me rest here for one night somehow. I shall leave tomorrow.” The man said, “Be off quickly, monk! Do not court death here!” Zhishen said, “How very strange! What harm could there be in resting here for one night? How could that be courting death?” The farmhand said, “Go when you are told. If you do not, we shall seize you and tie you up here.” Lu Zhishen flew into a rage. “You wretched bumpkin! What utter unreasonableness! I have said nothing offensive, yet you want to bind me!” Some of the farmhands cursed him, while others tried to restrain their fellows.

p.src: Lu Zhishen raised his monk’s staff and was just about to let his fury loose when an old man emerged from the manor. When Lu Zhishen looked at him, the old man appeared to be nearly sixty or perhaps older. Leaning on a staff taller than himself, the old man came forward and shouted at the servants, “What is all this commotion?” A servant said, “This monk is being utterly unreasonable and wants to beat us.” Zhishen promptly said, “This humble monk comes from Mount Wutai and is bound for the Eastern Capital on business. Tonight I failed to reach a lodging place and asked to spend one night at your honored manor, but that rude fellow wanted to bind me.” The old man said, “Since you are a monk from Mount Wutai, come inside with me.” Zhishen followed the old man straight into the main hall, where host and guest took their appointed seats. The old man said, “Reverend sir, please do not take offense. The servants did not understand that you came from a place of living Buddhas, and treated you as they would any ordinary person. I have always revered and believed in the Buddha, Heaven, and the Three Treasures. Though something is indeed happening at my manor tonight, I shall keep you here for one night before you go.” Zhishen leaned his monk’s staff aside, rose, and saluted with joined palms. “I am grateful for your kindness, benefactor. Might this humble monk venture to ask your honorable surname?” The old man said, “My surname is Liu. This place is called Peach Blossom Village, and the countryfolk all call me Old Master Liu of Peach Blossom Manor. May I ask your lay surname, Reverend, and by what religious name you are called?” Zhishen said, “My master is Abbot Zhizhen, and he bestowed a religious name upon me. Since my surname is Lu, I am called Lu Zhishen.” The old master said, “Reverend, please have some supper. I wonder whether you are willing to eat meat?” Lu Zhishen said, “I abstain from neither meat nor wine. Cloudy or clear, white wine or any other, I am not particular. Beef or dog meat—if there is any, I shall eat it.” The old master said, “Since you abstain from neither meat nor wine, I shall first have the servants bring some.” Before long, a servant carried in a table and set before Lu Zhishen a platter of beef, three or four vegetable dishes, and a pair of chopsticks. Zhishen removed his waist pouch and belly pouch and settled into his seat. The servant warmed a flask of wine, brought a cup, and poured wine for Zhishen to drink. Lu Zhishen offered no polite modesty and made no refusal. In no time at all, he had consumed the whole flask of wine and platter of meat. Watching him from across the table, the old master stared in amazement for a long while. The servant brought rice, and he ate that too. Then the table was carried away.

p.src: The old master instructed them, “Let the master rest for the night in the outer side room. If there is any commotion outside during the night, he must not come out to look.” Zhi-shen asked, “May I ask what is to happen at your manor tonight?” The old master replied, “It is no concern of a monk like you.” Zhi-shen said, “Why do you look so displeased, old sir? Can it be that you resent this poor monk for troubling you? Tomorrow I shall settle the price of my lodging with you, and that will be the end of it.” The old master said, “Listen, master. My household regularly feeds monks and gives alms; we would hardly begrudge provisions to one more monk. It is only that my young daughter is to take a husband tonight, and that is why I am distressed.” Lu Zhi-shen laughed heartily. “‘A grown man must wed, and a grown woman must marry.’ This is a great matter of human relations and one of the rites of the Five Constant Virtues. Why should it distress you?” The old master said, “You do not understand, master. This marriage is not one we consented to.” Zhi-shen laughed loudly. “Old sir, you are a fool yourself! If neither side consents, why take him into your household as a son-in-law?” The old master replied, “This old man has only this one young daughter, and she has just turned nineteen. Nearby stands a mountain called Peach Blossom Mountain. Lately, two chieftains have built a stockade there and gathered five or seven hundred men, who raid homes and rob travelers. The government troops here in Qingzhou have tried to suppress the bandits, but cannot restrain them. One of them came to my manor to demand tribute, saw my daughter, and left twenty taels of gold and one bolt of red brocade as betrothal gifts. He chose tonight as an auspicious date and is coming this evening to marry into my household. We cannot contend with him, so we have no choice but to give her to him. That is the cause of my distress; it is not that I begrudge lodging to you alone, master.”

p.src: When Zhi-shen heard this, he said, “So that is how matters stand. This poor monk has a way to make him change his mind and abandon the thought of marrying your daughter. What do you say?” The old master replied, “He is a fiend who kills without batting an eye. How could you possibly make him change his mind?” Zhi-shen said, “At the monastery on Mount Wutai, under the elder Zhi-zhen, I learned how to preach on causes and affinities. Even a man of iron and stone can be persuaded to turn around. Tonight, have your daughter hide elsewhere. I shall go into her chamber and preach to him about causes and affinities until he changes his mind.” The old master said, “That would be excellent indeed, but you must not go plucking a tiger’s whiskers.” Zhi-shen replied, “My life is mine to risk! You need only do as I say.” The old master said, “Then splendid! Our household is truly blessed to encounter a living Buddha descended to earth.” When the servants of the manor heard this, they were all startled.

p.src: The old master asked Zhi-shen whether he wanted any more rice. Zhi-shen replied, “I need no more rice, but if there is wine, bring me some more to drink.” The old master said, “There is, there is!” He at once ordered a servant to bring a cooked goose and pour wine into a large bowl. Zhi-shen drank his fill of twenty or thirty bowls and ate the whole cooked goose as well. He had a servant carry his bundle ahead and put it in the room, then took up his monk’s staff, girded on his戒刀, and asked, “Old sir, has your daughter gone into hiding yet?” The old master replied, “I have already sent my daughter to stay at a neighboring manor.” Zhi-shen said, “Lead me to the bride’s chamber.” The old master led him to the chamber and pointed. “It is in here.” Zhi-shen said, “Now all of you go and hide yourselves.” The old master and all the manor servants went outside to prepare the banquet. Zhi-shen moved the tables, chairs, and other furnishings in the room aside, placed his戒刀 at the head of the bed, leaned his monk’s staff beside it, lowered the gold-patterned bed curtains, stripped stark naked, and leapt onto the bed to sit.

On the threshing floor he had a table set out, with incense, flowers, lamps, and candles arranged upon it. Meanwhile, he had the servants heap meat upon large platters and warm wine in great pots. p.src: From shadows of green mountains locked in mist rolled forth a band of headless demons; Beside green woods veiled in smoke stood several ranks of hungry ghosts contending for food. Every man was fierce, each face hideous. Their headcloths were all madder-root red, their quilted coats all maple-leaf crimson. Paired tasselled spears encircled the little fiend who devoured men’s hearts and livers; Double cudgels clustered around the true Star of Calamity who cared neither for father nor mother. At night a rakshasa went to claim his bride; a mountain tiger came to dismount.

p.src: On his head he wore a dry-red, hollow-fronted cap drawn to a point, with an artificial flower of gauze and silk tucked beside his temple. Around his tiger’s frame was a green gauze robe embroidered in gold with tufted thread; around his wolfish waist, a red sash with a gold-patterned belly guard. On his feet were cloud-topped oxhide boots, and he rode a tall, curly-maned white horse.

p.src: When the chieftain reached the manor gate, he dismounted. All the young bandits shouted their congratulations in unison: “Your cap shines bright; tonight you shall be the bridegroom. Your garments fit trim; tonight you shall be the honored groom.” Old Master Liu hurriedly held up a tray and cup himself, poured a cup of fine wine, and knelt upon the ground. All the manor servants knelt as well. The chieftain reached out to raise him, saying, “You are my father-in-law. Why should you kneel to me?” The old master replied, “Do not say such a thing. This old man is merely a household under Your Majesty’s rule.” The chieftain was already seven or eight parts drunk. Laughing heartily, he said, “I shall become the son-in-law of your family, and that will do you no dishonor. Your daughter will be well matched with me.” Old Master Liu presented him with the cup offered upon dismounting. When they came to the threshing floor and he saw the incense, flowers, lamps, and candles, the chieftain said, “Father-in-law, why go to such trouble to welcome me?” There he drank another three cups, then entered the hall and ordered the young bandits to tether his horse to a green poplar tree. The young bandits began beating the drums and playing music before the hall. The chieftain took his seat in the hall and called, “Father-in-law, where is my lady?” The old master replied, “She is shy and does not dare come out.” The chieftain laughed. “Bring the wine first, and I shall return my father-in-law’s toast.” After drinking a cup, the chieftain said, “First I shall meet my lady. It will not be too late to come back and drink afterward.”

u.src: When the chieftain reached the manor gate, he dismounted. All the young bandits shouted their congratulations in unison: “Your cap shines bright; tonight you shall be the bridegroom.
Your garments fit trim; tonight you shall be the honored groom.”
Old Master Liu hurriedly held up a tray and cup himself, poured a cup of fine wine, and knelt upon the ground.
All the manor servants knelt as well.
The chieftain reached out to raise him, saying, “You are my father-in-law. Why should you kneel to me?”
The old master replied, “Do not say such a thing. This old man is merely a household under Your Majesty’s rule.”
The chieftain was already seven or eight parts drunk. Laughing heartily, he said, “I shall become the son-in-law of your family, and that will do you no dishonor.
Your daughter will be well matched with me.”
Old Master Liu presented him with the cup offered upon dismounting.
When they came to the threshing floor and he saw the incense, flowers, lamps, and candles, the chieftain said, “Father-in-law, why go to such trouble to welcome me?”
There he drank another three cups, then entered the hall and ordered the young bandits to tether his horse to a green poplar tree.
The young bandits began beating the drums and playing music before the hall.
The chieftain took his seat in the hall and called, “Father-in-law, where is my lady?”
The old master replied, “She is shy and does not dare come out.”
The chieftain laughed. “Bring the wine first, and I shall return my father-in-law’s toast.”
After drinking a cup, the chieftain said, “First I shall meet my lady. It will not be too late to come back and drink afterward.”

p.src: Old Master Liu’s sole hope was that the monk would persuade him, so he said, “This old man will lead Your Majesty there himself.” Taking a candlestick, he led the chieftain around behind the screen and straight to the bridal chamber. The old master pointed it out to him. “This is the room. Please enter by yourself, Your Majesty.” The old master took the candlestick and went straight away. Not knowing whether fortune or disaster would follow, he first made ready a path of escape.

p.src: The chieftain pushed open the chamber door and found it pitch-dark inside. The chieftain said, “Just look at my father-in-law! He is supposed to be a man of means, yet he has not even lit a lamp in the room and has left my lady sitting in the dark. Tomorrow I shall have the underlings carry down a whole barrel of good oil from the stronghold for her lamps.” Lu Zhishen, sitting inside the bed curtains, heard every word. He stifled his laughter and made not a sound. The chieftain felt his way into the room and called, “My dear, why do you not come out to welcome me? Do not be shy. Tomorrow you shall be my lady of the stronghold.” Calling out to his bride all the while, he groped this way and that. His hand found the gold-embroidered bed curtain. He lifted it, reached inside, and felt Lu Zhishen’s belly. Lu Zhishen seized the opportunity to grab him by his headcloth, knot and all, and with one thrust pinned him down beside the bed. Just as the chieftain tried to struggle free, Lu Zhishen clenched his right fist and cursed, “You filthy bastard!” He struck him once across the ear and neck. The chieftain cried, “Why are you beating your husband?” Lu Zhishen roared, “I will teach you to recognize your wife!” He dragged him down beside the bed and laid into him with fists and feet until the chieftain screamed for help. Old Master Liu was struck dumb with fright. He had supposed that by now the monk would be explaining the marriage bond and persuading the chieftain to change his mind, but instead he heard cries for help from within. In alarm, the old master took up a lamp and led the underlings rushing into the room. By the lamplight they saw a huge fat monk, stark naked without a thread upon him, straddling the fallen chieftain and beating him before the bed. The foremost underling shouted, “All of you, come save the chieftain!” The underlings all brandished spears and clubs and charged in to the rescue. Seeing them, Lu Zhishen released the chieftain, snatched up his Chan staff from beside the bed, sprang to the floor, and fought his way out. The underlings saw how fiercely he came at them, gave a shout, and all fled. Old Master Liu could do nothing but lament. Amid the uproar, the chieftain crawled out of the room and rushed to the gate. Finding his unsaddled horse, he broke a willow switch from a tree, leapt briskly onto its back, and lashed it with the switch, but the beast would not move. The chieftain cried, “What misery! Even this horse has turned against me!” Looking again, he realized that in his panic he had not untied the reins. He hastily tore them loose, mounted the bareback horse, and sped away. Once outside the manor gate, he cursed loudly, “Old donkey Liu, do not think this is over! You cannot fly away from me.” He gave the horse two cuts with the willow switch, and it bore the chieftain clattering away up the mountain.

p.src: Old Master Liu seized Lu Zhishen and said, “Monk, you have brought disaster upon my whole family!” Lu Zhishen said, “Forgive my discourtesy! First bring me my clothes and robe. Let me dress before we talk.” One of the household servants fetched them from the room, and Zhishen dressed. The old master said, “At first I only hoped you would explain the marriage bond and persuade him to change his mind. Who could have imagined that you would give him such a beating? He will surely return to the stronghold and bring a great band of outlaws to slaughter my family.” Zhishen said, “Do not be alarmed, old master. Let me tell you who I am. I am no ordinary man. I once served as a garrison major under the Elder Military Commissioner of Yan’an Prefecture, but after killing a man I entered the Buddhist order and became a monk. Never mind those two wretches—even if one or two thousand troops came against me, I would not fear them. If none of you believes me, try lifting my Chan staff.” The servants could not budge it. Zhishen took it from them and wielded it as lightly as if he were twirling a lamp wick. The old master said, “Master, please do not leave us. You must stay and protect our whole family.” Zhishen said, “What foolish talk! I would not leave even if it cost me my life.” The old master said, “Then let us bring the master some wine, but you must not drink yourself insensible.” Lu Zhishen replied, “With one measure of wine, I have one measure of skill; with ten measures, I have ten measures of strength.” The old master said, “If that is so, all the better. We have plenty of wine and meat here. Let the master eat and drink his fill.”

p.src: Now the chief leader of Peach Blossom Mountain sat in the stronghold, just about to send men down the mountain to learn how the second leader was faring as a bridegroom, when several underlings came rushing in, frantic and breathless, crying, “Disaster! Disaster!” The chief leader hurriedly asked, “What has happened to throw you into such a panic?” An underling answered, “Our second brother has been badly beaten.” The chief leader was greatly alarmed and had just begun asking for the details when someone reported, “The second brother is here.” The chief leader looked and saw that the second leader’s red headcloth was gone and his green robe had been torn to shreds. He dismounted, collapsed before the hall, and pleaded, “Brother, save me!” The chief leader asked, “What happened?” The second leader said, “Your brother went down the mountain, reached the old man’s manor, and entered the chamber. But curse that old donkey! He had hidden his daughter away and put a fat monk in her bed instead. I suspected nothing. When I lifted the curtain and reached in, that brute seized me and battered me with fists and feet until my whole body was covered in wounds. When the brute saw the others come in to rescue me, he let go, raised his Chan staff, and fought his way out. That was how I escaped and saved my life. Brother, you must see justice done and avenge me.” The chief leader said, “So that is what happened. Go to your room and recover. I shall go and seize that thieving baldhead for you.” Then he shouted to his attendants, “Quickly, saddle my horse!” All the underlings hurried off. The chief leader mounted, grasped his spear, and led every one of the underlings shouting down the mountain.

p.src: Now Lu Zhishen was still drinking when a manor servant reported, “Every one of the chief bandit’s men has come down from the mountain.” Zhishen said, “Do not panic. Whenever I knock one down, you need only bind him, hand him over to the authorities, and claim your reward. Bring me my戒刀.” Lu Zhishen stripped off his monk’s robe, hitched up the clothes beneath it, girded on his戒刀, and strode out to the threshing ground with his禪杖 in hand. There he saw the chief bandit charge through a mass of torches on horseback and rein in before the manor, his long spear leveled. He shouted, “Where is that bald donkey? Come out at once and let us settle who is the better man.” Zhishen flew into a rage and cursed, “You filthy, flog-worthy scoundrel! I will teach you who I am!” Swinging up his禪杖, he came sweeping it low along the ground. The chief held him at bay with his spear and cried, “Wait, monk—do not strike yet! Your voice sounds very familiar. Tell me your name first.” Lu Zhishen replied, “I am none other than Lu Da, formerly a major under the old Military Commissioner. Now I have entered the religious life and become a monk, and I am called Lu Zhishen.” The chief roared with laughter, tumbled from his saddle, cast aside his spear, and prostrated himself, saying, “Brother, I trust you have been well since we parted! No wonder my second brother fell into your hands.” Lu Zhishen thought it a trick and sprang several paces backward, abruptly checking his禪杖. Peering closely in the torchlight, he recognized none other than Li Zhong, the arms instructor and Tiger-Slaying General who had once wandered the rivers and lakes demonstrating spear and staff and selling medicines. It was the bandits’ custom not to use the ordinary word for bowing, since they considered it unlucky in military affairs; instead they called it jianfu, an auspicious expression. When Li Zhong rose from his bow, he took Lu Zhishen by the arm and asked, “Brother, how did you come to be a monk?” Zhishen said, “Come inside with me first, and we shall talk.” When Old Squire Liu saw this, he could only groan, “So this monk is one of their kind after all!”

p.src: Once inside, Lu Zhishen put his monk’s robe back on, and he and Li Zhong went to the hall to talk over old times. Lu Zhishen took the principal seat and called Old Squire Liu out, but the old man dared not come forward. Zhishen said, “Do not be afraid, Squire. He too is a brother of mine.” On hearing that the man was his brother, the old squire grew even more alarmed, yet dared not refuse to come out. Li Zhong sat in the second place, and the old squire in the third. Lu Zhishen said, “Since you are both here, listen. After I killed the Butcher of the West with three blows in Weizhou, I fled to Yanmen County in Daizhou, where I encountered Old Jin, whom I had given money for his journey. The old man had not returned to the Eastern Capital but had followed an acquaintance and settled in Yanmen County. His daughter had been given in marriage to a wealthy local gentleman named Squire Zhao. When we met, Squire Zhao treated me with the greatest respect. But the authorities were pressing the search for me so closely that the squire spent his own money to send me to Elder Zhizhen on Mount Wutai, where I had my head shaved and became a monk. After I twice caused an uproar in the monks’ hall while drunk, my master the elder gave me a letter and told me to go to the Great Xiangguo Monastery in the Eastern Capital, seek out Chan Master Zhiqing, and obtain a post among the working monks. Night overtook me, so I came to this manor seeking lodging, never imagining I would meet you here, brother. Who was the fellow I struck just now? And how did you come to be here?” Li Zhong replied, “After the three of us—you, Shi Jin, and I—parted that day at the tavern in Weizhou, I heard the next day that you had killed Zheng the Butcher. I went to look for Shi Jin and consult with him, but no one knew where he had gone. When I heard that officers were hunting us, I fled in haste as well and happened to pass beneath this mountain. The man you struck just now had already established a stronghold here on Peach Blossom Mountain. His name is Zhou Tong, the Little Conqueror. At the time he led his men down the mountain to fight me. I defeated him, and he asked me to remain on the mountain as chief of the stronghold, yielding the first chair to me. That is how I came to turn outlaw here.”

p.src: When the three had seated themselves, with Old Squire Liu standing before them, Lu Zhishen said, “Brother Zhou, listen to me. As for this marriage with Old Squire Liu’s family, you do not understand that he has only this one daughter. He depends entirely upon her to support him in old age, see him to his grave, and maintain the ancestral sacrifices. If you marry her, the old gentleman will be left without support, and how could he possibly consent in his heart? Take my advice: give her up and choose another good woman. The gold and satin originally agreed upon are here. What do you say?” Zhou Tong replied, “I shall obey every word you say, elder brother. I will never again go to their door.” Zhishen said, “When a true man gives his word, he must never go back on it!” Zhou Tong broke an arrow as his oath. Old Squire Liu bowed his thanks, took back the gold and satin, and descended the mountain to return to his manor.

p.src: Li Zhong and Zhou Tong slaughtered oxen and horses, laid on a feast, and entertained him for several days. They showed Lu Zhishen the scenery before and behind the mountain. Peach Blossom Mountain was indeed a fine stronghold, forbidding in form and steep on every side, with only a single path leading up and wild grass spreading everywhere below. After looking it over, Zhishen said, “This truly is a place of formidable natural defenses.” After staying several days, Lu Zhishen saw that Li Zhong and Zhou Tong were not generous men but miserly in all they did, and he insisted on leaving the mountain. The two begged him to remain, but he would not, merely protesting, “Now that I have become a monk, how could I consent to turn bandit?” Li Zhong and Zhou Tong said, “Since you will not turn bandit and mean to leave, elder brother, we shall go down the mountain tomorrow. Whatever we obtain, we will give it all to you for traveling expenses.” The next day, while sheep and pigs were slaughtered in the stronghold and a farewell banquet was being prepared, gold, silver, and wine vessels were set out upon the table. Just as they were about to take their seats and drink, a young bandit came to report, “Two carts and more than ten men are approaching below the mountain.” On hearing the report, Li Zhong and Zhou Tong mustered a large band of their men, leaving only one or two behind to attend Lu Zhishen at his wine. The two heroes said, “Please make yourself comfortable and drink a few cups, elder brother. We shall go down, seize some wealth, and return to see you on your way.” With these instructions given, they led their men down the mountain.

u.src: Li Zhong and Zhou Tong slaughtered oxen and horses, laid on a feast, and entertained him for several days.

They showed Lu Zhishen the scenery before and behind the mountain. Peach Blossom Mountain was indeed a fine stronghold, forbidding in form and steep on every side, with only a single path leading up and wild grass spreading everywhere below.
After looking it over, Zhishen said, “This truly is a place of formidable natural defenses.”
After staying several days, Lu Zhishen saw that Li Zhong and Zhou Tong were not generous men but miserly in all they did, and he insisted on leaving the mountain.
The two begged him to remain, but he would not, merely protesting, “Now that I have become a monk, how could I consent to turn bandit?”

Li Zhong and Zhou Tong said, “Since you will not turn bandit and mean to leave, elder brother, we shall go down the mountain tomorrow. Whatever we obtain, we will give it all to you for traveling expenses.”
The next day, while sheep and pigs were slaughtered in the stronghold and a farewell banquet was being prepared, gold, silver, and wine vessels were set out upon the table.
Just as they were about to take their seats and drink, a young bandit came to report, “Two carts and more than ten men are approaching below the mountain.”
On hearing the report, Li Zhong and Zhou Tong mustered a large band of their men, leaving only one or two behind to attend Lu Zhishen at his wine.
The two heroes said, “Please make yourself comfortable and drink a few cups, elder brother. We shall go down, seize some wealth, and return to see you on your way.”
With these instructions given, they led their men down the mountain.

p.src: Now Lu Zhishen reflected, “What misers those two are! Though all that gold and silver lies ready to hand, they will give me none of it, but insist on robbing someone else before making me a present. Is that not doing a favor at public expense, while making innocent people suffer? I shall give these fellows a fine surprise!” He called the few young bandits over to pour wine for him. He had drunk only two cups when he sprang up, felled two of the young bandits with his fists, untied his sash and bound them together with it, then stuffed their mouths with hemp and walnuts. Then he brought out his bundle and opened it, throwing away everything inessential. He took only the gold, silver, and wine vessels from the table, stamped them flat, and packed them into the travel-document pouch tied before his chest. He safely stowed away Elder Zhizhen’s letter; then he buckled on his monastic sword, took up his staff, balanced his clothes bundle on his head, and left the stronghold. At the rear of the mountain he looked out and saw only precipitous slopes. He thought, “If I leave by the front, I am certain to run into those fellows. Better to roll down through the wild grass here.” First he tied his sword and bundle together and threw them down the slope; then he hurled down his staff as well. Then he flung himself down and rolled over and over all the way to the foot of the mountain without suffering the least injury. A poem says:

A poem says:

p.src: So sheer the peril, not a bird-path opens; he longs to go, yet halts and doubts his way. Bald head and bundles tumble from the height, like ripened melons dropping from their stems.

p.src: Lu Zhishen, having rolled down the precipice, leaped to his feet, found his bundle, buckled on his sword, took up his staff, stretched his limbs, and set off along the road.

p.src: Meanwhile, Li Zhong and Zhou Tong reached the foot of the mountain and came face-to-face with those scores of men, each of whom carried a weapon. Li Zhong and Zhou Tong leveled their spears while the young bandits raised a battle cry. Rushing forward, they shouted, “You travelers there! If you know what is good for you, leave the road toll!” One of the travelers came forward with a woodcutter’s saber and fought Li Zhong. Back and forth they battled for more than ten bouts, neither gaining the advantage. Zhou Tong flew into a rage, charged forward with a shout, and all the young bandits attacked together. Unable to withstand them, the travelers turned and fled. Seven or eight of the slower men were all stabbed to death. Having seized the carts and their goods, the bandits sang songs of victory and leisurely climbed back up the mountain. When they reached the stronghold and looked around, they saw the two young bandits bound together beside a pavilion pillar. All the gold, silver, and wine vessels on the table had vanished. Zhou Tong untied the men and questioned them closely about what had happened and where Lu Zhishen had gone. The young bandits said, “He knocked the two of us down and bound us, swept up all those vessels, and took them away.” Zhou Tong said, “That thieving baldhead is no decent man! We have fallen victim to his tricks. But where did he go?” They searched everywhere for his tracks. At the rear of the mountain, they found a broad swath of wild grass flattened to the ground. Zhou Tong looked and said, “That bald donkey is an old hand at thieving! He rolled down from here, steep as this mountain ridge is.” Li Zhong said, “Let us catch him and demand our things back. We can humiliate the fellow as well.” Zhou Tong said, “Let it go, let it go! Shutting the gate after the thief has gone—where would we chase him? Even if we caught him, we could never get the things back. Should trouble arise, you and I could not defeat him; afterward it would only be awkward to meet again. Better to let the matter rest, so that we may meet on good terms in the future. For now, let us open the bundles on the carts and divide the gold, silver, and silks into three shares. You and I will each take one, and the third will reward our men.” Li Zhong said, “It was wrong of me to bring him up the mountain, causing you to lose so many things. I shall give you my entire share.” Zhou Tong said, “Elder brother, you and I share life and death. Do not calculate matters so closely.” Reader, remember where our tale has brought us: Li Zhong and Zhou Tong remained on Peach Blossom Mountain, carrying on their robberies at ease.

p.src: To return to Lu Zhishen: after leaving Peach Blossom Mountain, he strode on from morning until afternoon. Having covered some fifty or sixty li, he grew hungry, yet found no place along the road where he might obtain a cooked meal. He thought, “This morning I was so intent on getting away that I ate nothing. Where should I seek shelter now?” As he looked east and west, he suddenly heard the distant chiming of bells. Lu Zhishen exclaimed, “Excellent! If it is not a Buddhist monastery, it must be a Daoist temple—the wind is sounding the bells beneath its eaves. I shall seek it out and take refuge there.”

p.src: And when Lu Zhishen reached that place, fate decreed that more than ten living souls would lose their lives there, and that a single blaze would consume a renowned sacred mountain and its ancient monuments. Golden halls would glow with crimson flames, and black smoke rise before chambers of green jade. But what temple or monastery did Lu Zhishen seek? Listen to the explanation in the next installment.
